parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian accuratezza or French accuratesse.

18th century, from Italian broccoli, which see. The usual pronunciation with a long /oː/ is perhaps influenced by the French spelling brocoli, formerly also found in German texts. The sense of "marijuana" originated from a widely mocked quote said by the former German federal drug commissioner Danie

16th century as Bronzo, Brunzo, directly from Italian bronzo. Since the 18th century adapted to French bronze, itself from the Italian. Further origin uncertain; see the Italian lemma for more. The unusual pronunciation /s/ for ‹z› perhaps developed as a compromise between French /z/ and German /ts/

parole.significato: bust (sculptural portrayal of a person′s head and shoulders)
parole.testo: * The word was borrowed from Italian busto and French buste in the 18th century: More precisely, at the beginning of the 18th century the Busto and Buste were borrowed from Italian busto, and since the 2nd half of the 18th century, under influence of French buste which was also borrowed from Italian

parole.significato: personal effects, belongings that one carries with one (on one’s person or as luggage)
parole.testo: 17th century, borrowed from Italian effetti, then adapted (via forms like Effecti) to the German cognate Effekt (etymology 2 below). Usage was also influenced by French effets.

parole.significato: skirt suit (women’s business suit consisting of a skirt and jacket)
parole.testo: First borrowed in the early 18th century directly from Italian costume, which see. Later influenced by French costume, itself also from the Italian.

parole.significato: a sweet yeast bread prepared at Easter

parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian cittadella with influence from French citadelle. First attested in 1453, replacing earlier Schloss, and used alongside Stadtfestung or Stadtburg.
